System Change Is a Contact Sport!

There is a curious irony at the heart of the development sector's current obsession with "systems change." The people who talk about it most fluently are, by and large, the people who have changed the least. Their frameworks are immaculate. Their conference panels radiate conviction. And yet — nothing moves.

This is not an accident. It is a structural feature of how the sector rewards articulation over action, and proximity to power over proximity to the problem.
System change, in practice, is not a framework. It is an encounter. You go into a domain and you begin to push. And the system pushes back — not through abstract feedback loops but through the specific, maddening, occasionally illuminating (sometimes dangerous) resistance of real institutions, real incentives, and real people with real stakes in the status quo. That resistance is your teacher. The theory, if it ever becomes useful, comes later — excavated from the wreckage of your assumptions.

Most practitioners who have genuinely moved something will tell you the same thing: the leverage points they ended up using were not the ones they started with. The theory they have now was earned, not inherited.

You cannot have a credible opinion about a system you have no skin in. The development sector has industrialised the production of opinions about systems no one in the room is accountable to. Grant cycles end. White papers are published. The system, indifferent, continues.

The practitioner's version looks different. It is slower, messier, and almost never photogenic. It involves being wrong repeatedly and staying close enough to the consequence of being wrong that you are forced to correct. It involves the discipline of distinguishing between a theory of change that is intellectually satisfying and one that is operationally true.

The levers of any system are not visible from above. They are discovered through contact — through the specific friction of trying to shift something and learning, in that friction, what actually holds it in place. No literature review surfaces this. You find it by doing, by failing in instructive ways, and by staying in the room long enough to notice what changed.

This is not an argument against theory. It is an argument for the sequence: practice first, theory after, and humility always about the gap between the two.
The scoreboard for system change is not in the ecosystem. It is in the lives of people who had no say in whether the system got changed or not. That asymmetry — between those who theorise and those who absorb the consequences — is the one leverage point nobody puts on their framework.

What if an innovation ecosystem could enable more than just startups?

That’s the opportunity Mr. Raghuveer Kovuru sees as he takes on the role of Chief Executive Officer at VentureStudio.

His vision is to build at the intersection of 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐠𝐞, 𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩, helping students discover entrepreneurship, researchers take ideas beyond the lab, founders access the right ecosystem, and industry discover new possibilities within the university.

It’s about bringing together people, ideas and opportunities that might otherwise never meet.

And that is exactly what makes it exciting.

A meaningful exchange between two innovation ecosystems. 🇮🇳🇯🇵

We were delighted to welcome Hisashi Nakazawa, Director, Kobe Trade Information Office in Singapore, Kobe City Government, to VentureStudio, Ahmedabad University.

The visit offered an opportunity to explore how we support innovation from research and prototyping to incubation and commercialization, particularly across healthcare, life sciences and deep-tech.

During the visit, Mr. Nakazawa toured our three facilities and got a closer look at the infrastructure and capabilities available to innovators. He also interacted with our startups, gaining firsthand insights into the problems they are solving, their journeys, and the process of building and scaling from an academic ecosystem.

With Kobe’s strong biomedical, medical-device and biomanufacturing ecosystem, and Ahmedabad’s growing innovation and entrepreneurship landscape, there is significant potential for knowledge exchange, cross-border collaboration and stronger bridges between our two ecosystems.

Thank you, Mr. Nakazawa, for spending time with us and for the engaging conversations. We look forward to exploring what we can build together.
